conversation.content:
[Keating time note: sent Wednesday, November 18, 2026 at 2:19 PM EST; first message in this conversation.]
I drop one square tile into a bag, then add three round tiles. Before you explain, can I guess the shape I'm most likely to draw?

Good instinct to predict first — let's commit to an answer before I explain anything.

```openui lifecycle=ephemeral id=tile-draw-prediction

root = LearningSurface([guess], "Before the explanation", "Make a prediction, then I'll show why.", "ephemeral")
guess = Question([{ header: "Your prediction", question: "The bag holds 4 tiles: 1 square and 3 round. You reach in and draw one tile at random. Which shape are you most likely to draw?", type: "choice", choices: ["Square", "Round", "Both are equally likely", "There isn't enough information to say"], allowText: true, hint: "Think about how many of each shape are in the bag, not about the order they went in." }], "ephemeral", "Probability of a random draw", "Pick the shape you think is most likely — or write your own reasoning.")

```

content.text:
Exactly right — and your reasoning names the mechanism: probability here comes from **how many** tiles of each shape are in the bag, not from the order they went in.

Drawing one tile at random means every tile is equally likely to be the one you pull:

- Round: 3 of 4 tiles → **3/4 (75%)**
- Square: 1 of 4 tiles → **1/4 (25%)**

One nuance worth holding onto: the "drop one square, *then* add three round" sequence matters for nothing statistically. A bag doesn't remember order. If the tiles got jumbled in a bag, the order of insertion is irrelevant — only the counts are. (Order would only matter if you drew tiles one at a time *without* replacing them, which is a different experiment — and then you'd be far more likely to end up with round tiles overall too, since you're exhausting the bag.)

So: round is your best single guess, and it's a 3-to-1 edge over square.

Let me let you push on that number to check you believe it:

arguments.title: Tile draw probability explorer
arguments.description: An interactive explorer for drawing one tile at random from a bag. A slider sets how many round tiles are in the bag (there is always 1 square tile). Two readouts show the probability of drawing a round tile and of drawing a square tile, updating as the slider moves. A bar shows the two shares side by side. A simulation runs 1,000 random draws and reports how many of each shape actually came up, so the learner can compare the observed counts to the predicted probabilities.
arguments.html:
Bag of tiles: 1 square, some number of round

Move the slider, then run 1,000 draws to see whether the bag actually behaves the way the odds predict.
